lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI literacy means for students
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Define AI literacy in four student skills you can teach.
This lesson builds toward: For one grade you serve, you will describe the four student AI literacy skills in student-friendly words, with one example for each skill.
AI literacy is knowing enough about AI to use it well, question it and make good choices about it. For students, it comes down to four skills. Understand: AI predicts likely answers from patterns; it does not think or know like a person. Question: AI can be wrong, made up or biased, so check it.
Use: ask clear questions, use AI to learn (explain, quiz me, give feedback) rather than to avoid learning, and follow the class rules. Decide: think about privacy, fairness and honesty, such as what to share, whose work it is, and when not to use AI at all.
Grade matters. Younger students can learn the ideas with teacher demos and unplugged activities, without accounts. Older students can use approved tools directly under clear rules.
Words to know:
- AI literacy: knowing enough about AI to use it well, question it and make good choices.
- Unplugged activity: a lesson about technology that uses no devices.
Try it now: Write the four AI literacy skills in words your students would understand, for one grade you serve, with one example for each.
You can now define AI literacy as four teachable student skills.

options: Knowing how to build AI programs
Knowing enough about AI to use it well, question it and choose wisely
check.why: AI literacy is about using AI well and questioning it, not about coding.

check.q: Your second graders have no AI accounts. How would you teach AI literacy?
options: Have them sign up with a parent's account
Use teacher demos and unplugged activities
check.why: Demos and unplugged activities teach AI literacy without student accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A hands-on AI literacy lesson
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a 30-minute lesson where students test AI and catch its mistakes.
This lesson builds toward: Using an approved tool or a teacher demo, you will plan a 30-minute lesson where students test AI, catch an error and discuss bias, with five prepared questions tested beforehand, including one the AI gets wrong.
Students learn AI's limits best by seeing them. Structure: hook (5 minutes): ask "Is AI always right?" and take a vote. Investigate (15 minutes): in pairs, or through a teacher demo, ask an AI tool questions you prepared, including one it gets wrong or makes up (a fake source, a tricky math word problem, a local fact).
Fact-check (5 minutes): students check the answers against the textbook, a trusted website or the teacher. Discuss bias (5 minutes): ask the tool to describe "a scientist" or "a nurse" several times and notice patterns; talk about where those patterns come from.
Close with an exit ticket: "Name one thing AI is good for and one reason to check it." Test your prepared questions before class, because AI tools change and may fix or create errors.
Step by step:
- Hook: "Is AI always right?" vote.
- Investigate: prepared questions, including one it gets wrong.
- Fact-check against trusted sources.
- Discuss bias with a describe-a-person test.
- Exit ticket; test your questions before class.
Words to know:
- Fact-check: checking a claim against a trusted source.
- Bias: an unfair pattern, such as always describing a job as one kind of person.
Try it now: Prepare five questions for the lesson, including at least one the AI gets wrong. Test them in an approved tool and record the answers you will use.
You can now plan a hands-on lesson that teaches students to question AI.

check.q: What do students check AI answers against in the hands-on lesson?
options: The textbook, a trusted website or the teacher
Nothing; they trust the first answer
check.why: Trusted sources let students catch AI mistakes themselves.

check.q: The question you prepared to show an AI error now gets a right answer. What do you do?
options: Tell students AI never makes mistakes
Use it anyway and pretend it was wrong
Test other questions until you find one the AI gets wrong, and record the answers
check.why: AI tools change, so test questions shortly before the lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: AI as a learning partner, not an answer machine
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Teach students prompts that make AI help them think.
This lesson builds toward: On a topic you teach, you will write learning-partner prompts that make AI ask questions instead of giving answers, and explain why they help a student learn more than an answer-machine prompt.
The same tool can do a student's thinking or support it. The difference is the prompt. Answer machine: "Write my paragraph about the causes of the Civil War." Learning partner: "Ask me questions to help me figure out the causes, one at a time, and do not give me the answer."
Teach three learning-partner prompts: "Explain this another way, with an example"; "Quiz me on this and tell me what I got wrong"; "Here is my draft. Give me two strengths and one thing to improve, but do not rewrite it."
Some education tools are built to tutor this way. With any tool, students should check facts, and the work they hand in should be their own thinking, as the class AI use level allows.
Step by step:
- Show an answer-machine prompt and its result.
- Show a learning-partner prompt and its result.
- Teach three learning-partner prompts.
- Have students practice on today's topic.
- Remind: check facts; hand in your own thinking.
Words to know:
- Learning partner prompt: a prompt that asks AI to help you think rather than do the work.
- Socratic questioning: teaching by asking questions that lead the learner to reason it out.
Try it now: Try both an answer-machine prompt and a learning-partner prompt on a topic you teach. Write which one would help a student learn more and why.
You can now teach students to use AI to support their thinking, not replace it.

options: A prompt that asks AI to quiz you
A prompt that asks AI to do the work for you
A prompt that asks for hints
A prompt that asks AI to explain your mistakes
check.why: Answer-machine prompts skip the thinking the assignment builds.

check.q: A student wants AI help studying for a test. Which prompt would you teach?
options: "Quiz me one question at a time and tell me what I got wrong."
check.why: A learning-partner prompt keeps the student thinking.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Rules, safety and a school-wide plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: AI use levels for assignments
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set a five-level AI use scale and label assignments with it.
This lesson builds toward: Given your upcoming assignments, you will label each assignment with a level on a five-level AI use scale, with a reason tied to the learning goal.
Students need to know, for each assignment, what AI use is allowed. A simple five-level scale: Level 0, no AI. Level 1, AI for ideas only (brainstorm, then work on your own). Level 2, AI for feedback (on your own draft; you make the changes). Level 3, AI as a collaborator (you may use AI-generated parts, marked and explained). Level 4, AI exploration (using AI is the point of the task).
Label every assignment with its level, and explain why: a level 0 task might build a skill students must have on their own, like writing a timed paragraph or doing mental math. A level 2 task builds revision skills.
Use the same scale across the school so students do not face different rules in every class. Several published versions of AI assessment scales exist; adapt one or write your own with your staff.
Step by step:
- Agree a five-level scale with staff.
- Label each assignment with its level.
- Explain why that level fits the learning goal.
- Post the scale in class and online.
- Use the same scale across the school.
Words to know:
- AI use level: a label telling students how much AI they may use on a task.
- Collaborator: someone (or something) that works with you on a task.
Try it now: Write the five-level scale in student-friendly words. Then label five of your upcoming assignments with a level and a one-line reason.
You can now tell students clearly how much AI they may use on each task, and why.

check.q: What does Level 0 on the AI use scale mean?
options: AI may write the first draft
check.why: Level 0 is for tasks where students must show their own thinking without AI.

check.q: An assignment's goal is to practice writing a first draft alone. Which label fits?
options: Collaborator level, with AI drafting parts
A low level such as no AI, with the reason tied to that goal
The highest level, so students learn the tool
check.why: The level should fit the learning goal, with a reason students can see.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Saying how you used AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Teach students a simple way to disclose and cite AI use.
This lesson builds toward: When students use AI on allowed work, you will teach a one-line disclosure format for AI use, naming the tool, what it did, the date and what the student did.
Honesty about AI is a skill. When AI is allowed, students should say how they used it. A one-line disclosure works for most tasks: "I used [tool] to [what] on [date]. I [what I did with it]." For example: "I used Gemini to quiz me on vocabulary on March 3. I wrote all answers myself."
For research tasks, older students can follow the citation style your school uses; style guides such as MLA and APA publish guidance for citing AI tools on their own websites. AI is not a reliable source of facts, so students must still find and cite the original source.
Treat honest disclosure as a positive. Students who say what they did with AI are learning integrity; do not punish an honest disclosure of allowed use.
Step by step:
- Teach the one-line disclosure.
- Model it on your own AI-assisted work.
- For research, use your school's citation style guidance.
- Require original sources for facts.
- Praise honest disclosure.
Words to know:
- Disclosure: saying openly how you used AI.
- Citation: a note that tells the reader where information came from.
Try it now: Write a disclosure line for something you used AI for this week. Then write the instructions you will give students for disclosing AI use.
You can now teach students to disclose and cite AI use honestly.

check.q: What should a one-line AI disclosure include?
options: The tool, what it did, the date and what the student did
check.why: A full line shows exactly how AI was used.

check.q: A student honestly discloses allowed AI use on their work. How would you respond?
options: Treat the disclosure as a positive
check.why: Honest disclosure is the habit you want, so it should be welcomed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping students safe, and planning school-wide
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Teach student safety rules and plan AI literacy across grades.
This lesson builds toward: For students and families, you will explain the student AI safety rules and plan AI literacy across grades, in a half-page family letter covering the tools used, why, and the safety rules.
Teach students four safety rules. Do not share personal information (full name, address, school, photos, passwords) with AI tools. Use only tools the school has approved, under the age rules in the tool's terms. AI can create fake images, voices and videos (deepfakes): be careful what you believe and never create fakes of real people. Talk to a trusted adult if an AI conversation becomes upsetting, unsafe or asks for secrets.
For children under 13, COPPA applies to online services; the FTC says a school may consent for parents only when the service collects information for the school's use and benefit, with no other commercial purpose. Your district decides which tools students may use; tell families which ones and why.
Plan AI literacy by grade band, so each year builds on the last: early grades learn what AI is through demos; upper elementary practices questioning and fact-checking; middle school adds bias, disclosure and learning-partner use; high school adds ethics, careers and responsible creation. Share the plan with families.
Step by step:
- Teach the four safety rules.
- Confirm approved tools and age rules; for under 13, COPPA consent.
- Tell families which tools are used and why.
- Map AI literacy skills by grade band.
- Share the plan with families.
Words to know:
- Deepfake: a fake image, voice or video made with AI to look real.
- Grade band: a group of grades, such as K-2 or 6-8.
Official sources:
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Final task: assemble your student AI literacy package for one grade: the 30-minute lesson plan, the five-level AI use scale with an example assignment at each level, the one-line disclosure format, and a half-page family letter with the safety rules.
You can now lead student AI literacy with a lesson, clear use levels, honest disclosure and safety rules families understand.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Hands-on lesson Students do not test AI, catch an error or discuss bias. A 30-minute plan where students test an AI tool or watch a demo, catch an error and discuss bias. Prepared questions were tested beforehand and fit the grade. AI use scale Fewer than five levels, or levels without example assignments. A five-level scale with an example assignment at each level. Each example has a reason tied to the learning goal. Disclosure format No disclosure format, or it is missing key parts. A one-line format students will use to say how they used AI. Includes the tool, what it did, the date and what the student did, with an example. Family letter and safety No family letter, or the safety rules are missing. A half-page letter explaining what students will learn and the safety rules. Also says which tools are used and why, in plain words for families. Student-friendly literacy skills The package does not teach students to question AI. The lesson teaches students that AI can be wrong or biased and how to check it. Uses learning-partner prompts so AI helps students think. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A fake image, voice or video made with AI
check.why: Deepfakes are AI-made fakes, which is why students never create fakes of real people.

check.q: A student says an AI chat made them upset. What should they have been taught to do?
options: Delete the app and say nothing
check.why: Telling a trusted adult is one of the student safety rules.
